sideA.content: What is the purpose of dock lines during mooring?

sideB.content: To secure the vessel to the dock and control its movement.

lessons.title: Departing the Dock – What to Expect

content.content: As the boat prepares to leave the dock, your role may vary depending on experience and instruction. Understand what to expect and how to remain helpful and safe.

• Departure may involve engine use, sailing off a mooring, or pushing off from a slip.
• Crew may be assigned tasks like line handling, fender duty, or lookout.
• If you're not given a job, stay alert and out of the way.
• Once the boat is ‘clear of the dock,’ lines and fenders are stowed and we’re underway.

flashcards.title: FC: What to Expect During Departure

sideA.content: What are common ways a boat departs the dock?

sideB.content: By motoring, sailing off a mooring, or being pushed off from a slip.

content.content: Anchoring starts with understanding the seabed and wind direction.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Use visual cues and depth sounders to choose a safe location.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Scope and anchor type are critical to holding strength.

sideA.content: What factors determine a good anchoring spot?

sideB.content: Wind direction, seabed type, depth, and swing room.

content.content: Side ties are useful when rafting up with other boats.

Proper fender placement protects both vessels from contact damage.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Choose knots that are secure but easy to untie under load.

sideA.content: Why is fender placement critical during a side tie?

sideB.content: It prevents hull damage from contact with adjacent boats.

content.content: Slow and controlled movements are key when entering a slip.

Crew should be briefed and in position before final approach.

Use visual alignment with dock features to stay centered.

sideA.content: What should the crew do before the final docking approach?

sideB.content: Be briefed, ready in position, and aware of their tasks.

lessons.title: Basic Deck Safety and Boom Awareness

content.content: Always maintain three points of contact while on deck.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Watch the boom's position to avoid surprise jibes.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Secure loose lines and gear to prevent trip hazards.

sideA.content: What is the “three points of contact” rule?

sideB.content: Always have two hands and one foot (or vice versa) in contact with the boat for stability.

content.content: Crew should be stationed and aware of their docking role.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Lines should be coiled and ready to deploy quickly.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Communication between helm and crew is essential for timing.

sideA.content: What is a crew member’s main role when assisting with docking?

sideB.content: Be alert, positioned, and ready to handle lines on command.

content.content: Listen carefully to helm commands and anticipate needs.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Ensure the anchor is free to drop and flaked correctly.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Watch for signs of dragging or improper setting.

sideA.content: What should crew do before dropping the anchor?

sideB.content: Verify the anchor is ready and listen for commands.

content.content: Approach into the wind and stop the boat before dropping anchor.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Let the rode out steadily to avoid tangles.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Observe how the anchor sets and adjust scope if necessary.

sideA.content: Why do you approach into the wind when anchoring?

sideB.content: To reduce drift and improve anchor set accuracy.

content.content: Coordinate engine movement with winch operation to reduce strain.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Ensure crew hands are clear of the windlass during retrieval.
assets/images/fallback_image.jpeg
Secure the anchor and check it's seated properly before departure.

sideA.content: Why is it important to coordinate engine and winch when raising anchor?

sideB.content: To reduce load on the windlass and avoid damaging gear.
